lines.text: A rainforest land on South America's coast, shaped by Dutch plantations, Maroon freedom and peoples from three continents. This is Suriname.
It begins with Paramaribo, a trading post from 1613. Its old Dutch wooden centre is now a World Heritage Site.
In 1667 the Dutch kept Suriname in a treaty with England, which kept New Amsterdam, later New York.
For two centuries enslaved Africans worked its plantations. On the first of July 1863, slavery was finally abolished.
Desi Bouterse, born in 1945, would become the soldier who seized power, and much later was elected president.
Jennifer Geerlings-Simons, born in 1953, would become the country's first woman president in 2025.
In November 1975, after more than three centuries as a Dutch colony, Suriname became an independent nation.
The next year, Clarence Seedorf was born in Paramaribo. He would become one of the great midfielders of European football.
But in 1980 Bouterse led a coup, and in December 1982 fifteen opponents of the military regime were killed.
In 1998 a vast reserve of untouched rainforest was set aside in the heart of the country.
From plantations to a free nation of many peoples, Suriname is still writing its story.
